analysis.one_liner: Requires oil companies to prove they can prevent and stop a well blowout before drilling high-risk wells.
analysis.headline: Passed out of the House Energy and Commerce Committee unanimously, 48-0, but never received a vote in the full House or Senate and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after the Deepwater Horizon disaster, this bill would have barred companies from drilling offshore or other high-risk oil and gas wells unless they proved in advance that their blowout preventer would work, that they could contain a blowout if equipment failed, and that they could quickly drill a relief well. It also required independent third-party testing of blowout preventers, unannounced federal inspections, big fines for violations, whistleblower protections for oil workers, and new powers for safety investigators. The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved it unanimously, but it never came to a vote in the full House or Senate and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing and tourism businesses, offshore oil workers, and taxpayers who otherwise shoulder cleanup and economic damage from oil spills. A repeat of the Deepwater Horizon disaster — 11 workers killed and months of oil pouring into the Gulf — becomes less likely because companies must prove containment capability and relief-well capacity before drilling, equipment must pass independent certification, and workers who flag dangers gain legal protection from retaliation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, fishermen, offshore workers, taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: No drilling permit for a high-risk well unless the company proves its blowout preventer will work, it can stop a blowout if equipment fails, and it can drill a relief well quickly — the failure that turned Deepwater Horizon into a months-long spill.

Mandates redundant blind shear rams and casing shear rams, backup control systems, independent third-party certification and 180-day recertification of blowout preventers, and real-time transmission of blowout preventer control logs to regulators.

Requires safe well design and cementing certified by independent third parties, stop-work authority when a blowout is imminent, unannounced inspections, and civil penalties up to $150,000 per day plus criminal penalties including personal liability for corporate officers.
Protects oil workers from being fired for reporting safety violations, and gives citizens the right to sue to enforce the law.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies drilling offshore or other high-risk wells: they would pay certification and inspection fees, install redundant blowout preventer equipment, attest personally through their CEOs, and face civil penalties up to $150,000 per day and criminal penalties up to $10 million and 10 years in prison for willful violations. Some of those costs would likely be passed to consumers through energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil and gas drilling companies

drawbacks.text: The bill layers pre-drilling certifications, recertifications every 180 days, and federal inspections on top of existing permitting, which would add cost and time to offshore drilling projects; critics could argue it slows energy production.

The relief-well requirement — begin drilling within 15 days and complete within 90 days of a blowout — and detailed engineering mandates were described in the bill itself as potentially requiring drilling a relief well in tandem, which the bill ordered the National Academy of Engineering to study for economic impact, acknowledging the requirement could be costly.
Penalties of up to $150,000 per day and criminal exposure of up to 10 years for executives add legal risk to operators, which opponents could argue raises the cost of domestic drilling.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — a lower chance of another months-long underwater oil gusher, real containment capability, and protections for workers who report unsafe conditions — are large and the costs (certification and inspection fees on oil companies, slower permitting) fall mainly on a wealthy industry. The main honest drawback is that heavy pre-drilling certification requirements could slow or deter offshore drilling, raising energy costs, and there is no evidence in the record of how those tradeoffs would balance out. The bill was reported unanimously by a committee that included Republicans, suggesting the safety case was broadly accepted.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved it unanimously in July 2010, but no further action was ever taken and it died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced June 29, 2010, in response to the Deepwater Horizon blowout, and referred to the Natural Resources and Energy and Commerce Committees.
On July 15, 2010, the Energy and Commerce Committee ordered it reported as amended by a vote of 48-0 with one member voting present, and it was formally reported on July 29, 2010 (H. Rept. 111-581).
After being reported to the House, the bill received no floor action and was never considered by the Senate; it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drillers avoided new certification, inspection, and equipment costs, and offshore drilling regulation stayed as it was.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through committee to a unanimous 48-0 reported vote.

for.name: Energy and Commerce Committee (48 members voting)
for.what_they_did: Voted 48-0 (one present) to report the bill amended to the House floor on July 15, 2010.

for.name: Reps. Edward Markey and Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Joined Waxman in introducing the bill.

against.name: House leadership (111th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the committee-approved bill to the House floor for a vote, and it was never taken up in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: The committee reported the bill unanimously 48-0 with one member voting present, so the record shows no partisan split in committee; the obstacle was the absence of floor action rather than a recorded vote against it.

industries.industry: Offshore and high-risk oil and gas drillers
industries.note: They would bear new certification, inspection, and equipment costs ($75,000–$150,000 per day in civil penalties for violations) and CEO-level attestation duties, and drilling would stop whenever a blowout risk appeared. These are the parties whose cost-cutting failures produced the Deepwater Horizon disaster.

industries.industry: Independent third-party inspection and certification firms
industries.note: The bill creates a new market: federally assigned, federally contracted certifiers for every blowout preventer and well design, paid for by operator fees.

industries.industry: Oilfield service and equipment makers (blowout preventer manufacturers)
industries.note: New redundancy and testing standards would force redesign and create demand for upgraded equipment, but raise compliance costs.
